units.la: Ν̄δρες ἡύςυλοι, σύ θ' ὅτεώ γε κλιτόν Τοῦνομ' εἰςιλὼν ἐςατὴ ἔδωκεν, Τοῦ Διέςυς πλήσει μελέτας ἀεύεςαν Ἡχέτα τέτλιξ.
units.tr: Men, who are fond of the Muses, and you, whoever you are, who have been given a name by your fate, the Muses' favour, you have been filled with ever-lasting care [Ν̄δρες ἡύςυλοι, σύ θ' ὅτεώ γε κλιτόν Τοῦνομ' εἰςιλὼν ἐςατὴ ἔδωκεν, Τοῦ Διέςυς πλήσει μελέτας ἀεύεςαν Ἡχέτα τέτλιξ].

units.la: Λήιον δ' ἤδη φερέμεν κ' ἐγῷδα Ἐρχάτην μύεμηκα, λέγω. τελώςης Ἐρξάπν δὲν μέλιλ⊙ μέλιστὰν Τάνδτεκ γαίης.
units.tr: Already I know how to bring in the grain, I say; the harvest of the land is ready for the one who has reaped it [Λήιον δ' ἤδη φερέμεν κ' ἐγῷδα Ἐρχάτην μύεμηκα, λέγω. τελώςης Ἐρξάπν δὲν μέλιλ⊙ μέλιστὰν Τάνδτεκ γαίης].

units.la: Ἀλλ' ἂν ἔλθῃσι χρυσροῖο ὤρη Χείμα⊙, κ' οὔσης σκιερῆς ὀπωρης, Ἀλέγης τέτλιξ ἄπορεῖ ἐδωδῆς Τοῖσδε φάγοντι.
units.tr: But if the golden hour of winter comes, and autumn is shady, the wretched man has no food for the one who eats these things [Ἀλλ' ἂν ἔλθῃσι χρυσροῖο ὤρη Χείμα⊙, κ' οὔσης σκιερῆς ὀπωρης, Ἀλέγης τέτλιξ ἄπορεῖ ἐδωδῆς Τοῖσδε φάγοντι].

units.la: Ἐπομαι απουδὴ ὃ ἐγὼν μελίτης. Ἄνδρες, ὡς καρπῶν λαβέειν, ἀξεσοι, Ἱερῶτα μοισάων χρεὸς ιερέων Λίσετ' ὑμμας.
units.tr: I follow the study which I pursue. Men, so that you may gather the fruits, the sacred Muses have set you apart as priests of their rites [Ἐπομαι απουδὴ ὃ ἐγὼν μελίτης. Ἄνδρες, ὡς καρπῶν λαβέειν, ἀξεσοι, Ἱερῶτα μοισάων χρεὸς ιερέων Λίσετ' ὑμμας].

units.la: Valentinus Reusius, Resp.
units.tr: Valentinus Reusius, respondent.

units.la: Theses Physicae DE SUBJECTO PHYSICES.
units.tr: Physics Theses: ON THE SUBJECT OF PHYSICS.

units.la: Thesis I.
units.tr: Thesis I.

units.la: Cum inter tot nobilissimas quaestiones, ab Aristotelis interpretibus ἄνω καὶ κάτω ventilatas, haec neutiquam, quae de physices subjecto agitata est, sit minima, non me [?]ἀνολογεῖν ἢ ἀεὶ[?]ςᾶτεῖν arbitror, si, quid hic statuendum videatur, brevibus expediam.
units.tr: Since, among so many most noble questions debated with great vigour by the interpreters of Aristotle, this one, which concerns the subject of physics, is by no means the least, I do not think I am [ἀνολογεῖν ἢ ἀεὶ ςᾶτεῖν] if I briefly set out what seems to be decided here.

units.la: 2. Non enim haec quaestio nullius momenti existimanda est, quippe quae ad naturam Physiologiae venandam, maximè sit necessaria.
units.tr: 2. For this question should not be thought of as of no moment, since it is most necessary for discovering the nature of physiology.

units.la: 3. Cùm enim scientia naturalis una sit, & unitas scientiae sumatur ex unitate subjecti, unum totius philosophiae naturalis subjectum adaequatum constituatur, oportet.
units.tr: 3. For since natural science is one, and the unity of a science is taken from the unity of its subject, one adequate subject of the whole of natural philosophy must be established.

units.la: 4. Quodnam hoc statuendum sit, vehementer inter Aristotelis interpretes olim disceptatum fuit.
units.tr: 4. What this subject should be has long been vehemently disputed among the interpreters of Aristotle.

units.la: 5. Ego, priore loco dissentientibus philosophorum opinionibus expositis, deinde, quid veritati magis consentaneum sit, dispiciam.
units.tr: 5. I will first set out the opinions of the philosophers who disagree, and then examine what is more consistent with the truth.

units.la: 6. Primùm autem se nobis offert Thomas Aquinas, qui in principio primi lib. phys. asserit, ens mobile esse subjectum physices.
units.tr: 6. First, Thomas Aquinas presents himself, who at the beginning of the first book of the Physics asserts that the mobile being is the subject of physics.

units.la: 7. Hanc suam sententiam, ut sartam tectam retineat, hoc inprimis argumento suadere conatur.
units.tr: 7. To keep this opinion intact, he tries to persuade by this argument above all.

units.la: 8. Subjectum Physicae, aut est corpus mobile, aut est ens mobile.
units.tr: 8. The subject of physics is either a mobile body or a mobile being.

units.la: 9. At corpus mobile nullo modo esse potest. Ergo.
units.tr: 9. But a mobile body cannot be in any way. Therefore [the subject is not a mobile body].

units.la: 10. Assumtum duplici modo stabilire nititur.
units.tr: 10. He tries to establish the assumption in two ways.

units.la: 11. Primùm: quia subjectum adaequatum, omnes res in scientia propositas sub se complecti debet.
units.tr: 11. First: because the adequate subject must comprehend under itself all the things treated in the science.

units.la: 12. Sub corpore autem, inquit, principia rerum naturalium, affectiones & accidentia, contineri non possunt.
units.tr: 12. But, he says, the principles of natural things, their affections and accidents, cannot be contained under body.

units.la: 13. Secundùm: quia, si corpus mobile physices subjectum esset, probaretur subjectum in sua scientia, quod dicendum non est.
units.tr: 13. Second: because, if the mobile body were the subject of physics, the subject would be proved within its own science, which must not be said.

units.la: 14. Aristoteles autem 6. phys. probat, omne mobile esse dividuum quod est probare, omne mobile esse corpus.
units.tr: 14. But Aristotle, in the sixth book of the Physics, proves that every mobile is divisible, which is to prove that every mobile is a body.

units.la: 15. Quoniam ergo physicus corpus mobile esse probat, idem physices subjectum constitui nullo modo potest.
units.tr: 15. Since, therefore, the physicist proves that the mobile is a body, the same cannot in any way be established as the subject of physics.

units.la: 16. Verum ad priorem assumti confirmationem respondetur, eatenus de principiis & affectionibus in physicis tradi, quatenus videlicet corpori naturam habenti insunt: Hoc enim sublato, neque principia, neque affectiones remanebunt: utpote quae subjecti principia sunt, & in eo cum traduce haerent.
units.tr: 16. But to the first confirmation of the assumption it is answered that principles and affections are treated in physics only so far as they inhere in a body having nature; for if this is removed, neither principles nor affections will remain, since they are principles of the subject and cling to it along with its nature.

units.la: 17. Ad posteriorem assumti probationem ex 6. phys. allatam, facilis etiam est responsio: quia, licet co loci ostendatur, omne mobile esse divisum, non tamen ob id probatur, dari corpus mobile.
units.tr: 17. The answer to the second proof of the assumption, drawn from the sixth book of the Physics, is also easy: for although it is shown in that passage that every mobile is divided, it is not therefore proved that there is a mobile body.

units.la: 18. Cum ergo dividuum esse, & corpus mobile esse, non sit idem, facile cuivis mediocriter oculato apparet, hanc Thomae probationem non procedere, quippe non omne, quod est divisibile, statim etiam est corpus.
units.tr: 18. Since, then, being divisible and being a mobile body are not the same, it is plain to anyone moderately sharp-sighted that this proof of Thomas does not hold, for not everything that is divisible is at once a body.

units.la: 19. Siquidem linea & superficies dividuae sunt, neque tamen ob id sunt corpora, ut recte infert Zab. lib. de natur. scient. constit. pag. 8.
units.tr: 19. For a line and a surface are divisible, and yet they are not therefore bodies, as Zabarella rightly infers in his book on the constitution of natural science, p. 8.

units.la: 20. Unde etiam idem Thomas, videns argumenti sui vanitatem in principio 1. lib. de caelo, corpus mobile esse subjectum, asserit.
units.tr: 20. Hence Thomas himself, seeing the emptiness of his argument, asserts at the beginning of the first book On the Heavens that the subject is a mobile body.

units.la: 21. Quae eadem etiam Alberti Magni opinio fuit, tractat. I. c. 3.
units.tr: 21. This was also the opinion of Albert the Great, treatise I, ch. 3.

units.la: 22. Hanc suam opinionem, ut probabilem reddat, duabus potissimum utitur rationibus.
units.tr: 22. To make this opinion appear probable, he uses chiefly two reasons.

units.la: 23. Una: Illud est subjectum scientiae, cujus partes & causae in scientia considerantur.
units.tr: 23. One: that is the subject of a science whose parts and causes are considered in the science.

units.la: 24. At corporis mobilis partes, nempe materia & forma, considerantur in physica. Ergo.
units.tr: 24. But the parts of a mobile body, namely matter and form, are considered in physics. Therefore [the mobile body is the subject].

units.la: 25. Altera subjectum debet esse tale, ut scientiam non excedat.
units.tr: 25. The other: the subject must be such that it does not exceed the science.

units.la: 26. At ens mobile competit etiam Angelis. Ergo.
units.tr: 26. But the mobile being belongs also to the angels. Therefore [the mobile being exceeds physics].

units.la: 27. Quae sententia, si sano modo intelligatur, nostra non repugnabit.
units.tr: 27. This opinion, if it is understood in a sound sense, will not conflict with ours.

units.la: 28. Nam τὸ mobile Alberto significat idem, quod naturale, habens in se principium motus & quietis.
units.tr: 28. For by "mobile" Albert means the same as "natural", that is, having within itself a principle of motion and rest.

units.la: 29. Tertia opinio est Scoti, qui physices subjectum substantiam naturalem statuit.
units.tr: 29. The third opinion is that of Scotus, who holds that the subject of physics is natural substance.

units.la: 30. Hujus sententia autoritate Aristotelis in principio 3. de caelo nititur. nitítur, ubi physicum circa substantiam versari, ait.
units.tr: 30. He rests this opinion on the authority of Aristotle in the beginning of the third book On the Heavens, where he says that the physicist is concerned with substance.

units.la: 31. Aristoteles autem loco dicto substantias corporeas intelligit: quod inde patet, quòd statim eas recensens, sola corpora nominet.
units.tr: 31. But Aristotle, in the place cited, understands corporeal substances; this is clear from the fact that, in enumerating them immediately afterwards, he names only bodies.

units.la: 32. Ultima, eaq; verißima est sententia recentiorum, in quam omnes hac ætate videntur conspirasse: subjectum physices esse corpus universè sumtum, quod & cœlestia, & inferiora omnia complectatur, quatenus naturale, hoc est, quatenus habet in seipso naturam, qua motus principium esse definitur.
units.tr: 32. The last opinion, and the truest, is that of the recent writers, in which all in this age seem to have agreed: that the subject of physics is body taken universally, which embraces both the heavenly and all the lower things, insofar as it is natural, that is, insofar as it has within itself a nature, which is defined as a principle of motion.

units.la: 33. Subjectum autem duabus constabit partibus, teste Zab. 1. de natur. Log. & lib. de præcognit. re consideratâ, quæ hic est corpus: & modo considerandi, quâ naturale.
units.tr: 33. The subject, however, will consist of two parts, as Zabarella teaches in his first book On the Nature of Logic and in his book On Previous Knowledge Considered: the thing, which here is body, and the mode of considering it, by which it is natural.

units.la: 34. Hanc sententiam haud dubiè veram esse censemus, cùm & efficaci ratione, & doctiß. physicorum testimoniis comprobetur.
units.tr: 34. We judge this opinion to be undoubtedly true, since it is confirmed both by a convincing argument and by the testimonies of the most learned physicists.

units.la: 35. Ratio hæc est: Illud est statuendum subjectum, cui omnes conditiones, quas Aristoteles in post. analyt. in cujusq; scientiæ subjecto requirit, competunt.
units.tr: 35. The argument is this: that must be established as the subject to which all the conditions that Aristotle requires in the subject of each science in the Posterior Analytics belong.

units.la: 36. At hæ competunt omnes corpori naturam habenti.
units.tr: 36. But all these belong to a body having nature.

units.la: 37. Assumtum sic ostenditur.
units.tr: 37. The assumption is shown as follows.

units.la: 38. Conditiones hæ sunt: 1. Subjecti esto anticipata notio, id est, subjectum debet ita esse præcognitum, ut intelligamus, & τί ἔστι τὸ σημαινόμενον, & ὅτι ἔστι.
units.tr: 38. These conditions are: (1) the subject should have a prior notion, that is, the subject must be known beforehand so that we understand both what the name signifies [τί ἔστι τὸ σημαινόμενον] and that it is [ὅτι ἔστι].

units.la: 39. II. Subjectum omnibus, quæ in scientia considerantur, substratum esto, ut ipsum nulli insit.
units.tr: 39. (2) The subject should be a substratum of all the things considered in the science, so that it inheres in none.

units.la: 40. III. Subjectum habeto principia, & accidentia demonstranda.
units.tr: 40. (3) The subject should have principles and accidents to be demonstrated.

units.la: 41. IV. Subjectum καθολικὸν, id est, toti scientiæ adæquatum esto, ut neq; eam excedat, neq; ab ea excedatur.
units.tr: 41. (4) The subject should be universal [καθολικὸν], that is, adequate to the whole science, so that it neither exceeds the science nor is exceeded by it.

units.la: 42. Jam verò corpus naturam habens, primùm præcognoscitur, tùm quid nomen significet, tùm quod sit.
units.tr: 42. Now a body having nature is first known beforehand, both as to what the name signifies and that it is.

units.la: 43. Secundò: Nulli inest, cùm ipsum per se subsistat, sed ipsum omnibus in physicis consideratis substratum est.
units.tr: 43. Second: it inheres in nothing, since it subsists through itself, but it is a substratum of all the things considered in physics.

units.la: 44. Tertiò: Habet principia & accidentia, quæ de ipso demonstrantur.
units.tr: 44. Third: it has principles and accidents, which are demonstrated of it.

units.la: 45. Quartò: Est toti physicæ adæquatum: nulla enim huius scientiæ pars est, in qua non agatur de principio, aut de accidente aliquo corporis naturæ naturalis, quâ tale, id est, quâ corruptioni obnoxium est: & nulla alia est scientia, in qua de jam dictis etiam tradatur.
units.tr: 45. Fourth: it is adequate to the whole of physics. For there is no part of this science in which something is not treated concerning a principle or some accident of natural body, as such, that is, insofar as it is subject to corruption; and there is no other science in which the things just mentioned are also taught.

units.la: 46. Ergò corpus naturale, quâ tale, est hujus scientiæ subjectum.
units.tr: 46. Therefore natural body, as such, is the subject of this science.

units.la: 47. Testimonia philosophi colligantur ex 2. phys. 1. & 3. de cælo. 6. Metaphys.
units.tr: 47. The testimonies of the philosopher are gathered from the second book of the Physics, the first book On the Heavens, and the sixth book of the Metaphysics.

units.la: 48. Huc redeunt sententiæ Thomæ, Alberti, & Scoti, si candidè explicentur.
units.tr: 48. The opinions of Thomas, Albert, and Scotus come to this, if they are candidly explained.

units.la: 49. Restant jam aliorum opiniones, de quibus etiam breviter dicemus.
units.tr: 49. There remain now the opinions of others, which we will also briefly discuss.

units.la: 50. Hi autem in duas sectas distincti esse videntur: aliqui enim communius aliquod corpore naturali: aliqui etiam eodem angustius subjectum introduxerunt. Utrumque vitiosum.
units.tr: 50. These seem to be divided into two sects: for some have introduced something more general than natural body, and others have introduced a narrower subject than body. Both are faulty.

units.la: 51. Qui communius finxerunt, quamlibet essentiam (ut incorpoream etiam, Deum & angelos) physices subjectum constituerunt.
units.tr: 51. Those who devised a more general subject have made any essence whatever (even an incorporeal one, such as God and the angels) the subject of physics.

units.la: 52. Communius hoc est, quia substantia materia expertes, seu formæ separatæ pertinent ad Musieum Metaphysicum.
units.tr: 52. This is too general, because substances free of matter, or separate forms, belong to metaphysics.

units.la: 53. Qui verò angustius, vel corpus caducum, (cælum excludentes) vel corpus naturale mistum (& cælum, & elementa excludentes) naturalis scientiæ subjectum fecerunt.
units.tr: 53. Those who made the subject narrower, either a perishable body (excluding the heavens), or a mixed natural body (excluding both the heavens and the elements), have made it the subject of natural science.

units.la: 54. Angustius hoc est, quia non tantum corpori caduco, sed etiam cælo & elementis naturæ notio ac definitio convenit.
units.tr: 54. This is too narrow, because the notion and definition of nature apply not only to perishable body but also to the heavens and the elements.

units.la: 55. Atque hæc de præsenti [illegible, ~8 letters] dicta sufficiant.
units.tr: 55. Let these things said about the present [illegible] suffice.

units.la: Ethicæ.
units.tr: Ethics

units.la: 1. Inter virtutes [illegible, ~6 letters], tanquam lumen quoddam emicat Comitas seu Affabilitas.
units.tr: 1. Among the virtues [illegible], Courtesy or Affability shines forth like a certain light.

units.la: 2. Ea enim facit, ut dicta & facta nostra aliquando, quasi quodam sale humanitatis, aspergantur & condiantur.
units.tr: 2. For it makes our words and deeds, as it were with a certain salt of humanity, sometimes seasoned and flavoured.

units.la: 3. De hac igitur breviter disseremus.
units.tr: 3. Therefore we shall discuss this briefly.

units.la: 4. Est autem affabilitas virtus, inter assentationem & contentionem posita, quæ in jucunditatibus molestiùs cernitur, quæ ex colloquiis hominum oriuntur.
units.tr: 4. Affability is a virtue placed between flattery and contentiousness, which is more troublesome to observe in the pleasantries that arise from people's conversations.

units.la: 5. Extremæ ejus sunt adulatio, quæ ex incessu, & morositas, seu contentio, quæ in defectu peccat. 6. Adulatio est vitiosus habitus loquendi placentia. Vel, est vitium, quo tanquam novo aucupio hominum gnathonici, sui ventis potissimum causa utuntur.
units.tr: 5. Its extremes are flattery, which goes wrong by excess, and moroseness, or contentiousness, which errs by defect. 6. Flattery is a vicious habit of speaking so as to please. Or, it is a vice by which flatterers, as with a new kind of bird-catching of men, use people chiefly for the sake of their bellies.

units.la: 7. Blandus & placendi studiosus Graecis dicitur ἀρεσκος, qui omnibus, quae dicuntur & fiunt, applaudit, omniaq; laudat.
units.tr: 7. A man who is fawning and eager to please is called in Greek areskos [ἀρεσκος], one who applauds everything that is said or done and praises all of it.

units.la: 8. Morositas est perversus habitus animi, cum quispiam omnibus contradicit, hoc unum agens, ut aliis sua difficultate molestiam pariat.
units.tr: 8. Moroseness is a perverse habit of mind, when someone contradicts everyone, doing this one thing alone, that he may cause annoyance to others by his difficult temper.

units.la: 9. Morosus Graecis dicitur δυσχερὴς, contentiosus & difficilis.
units.tr: 9. The morose man is called in Greek dyskherēs [δυσχερὴς], contentious and difficult.

units.la: Corollaria.
units.tr: Corollaries

units.la: 1. Optativo, quem vocant, modo Latinos carere dicimus.
units.tr: 1. We say that the Latins lack what is called the optative mood.

units.la: 2. Definitio verbi, qua definitur vox significans agere aliquid, aut pati, non est bona.
units.tr: 2. The definition of the verb, by which it is defined as a word signifying to do or to suffer something, is not good.

units.la: 3. Divisionem verbi in personale, & impersonale, tanquam supervacuam rejicimus.
units.tr: 3. We reject the division of the verb into personal and impersonal as superfluous.

units.la: 4. Evocatio Grammaticorum nulla est.
units.tr: 4. The "evocation" of the grammarians is nothing.

units.la: 5. Inepta est pronunciatio haec, aliquando, deinde, perinde, accentu videlicet in antepenultimam rejecto.
units.tr: 5. This pronunciation is faulty: aliquando, deinde, perinde, namely with the accent thrown back onto the antepenultimate syllable.

units.la: 6. Errant, qui Trinitatis mysterium in agrum physicum serunt.
units.tr: 6. Those err who sow the mystery of the Trinity in the field of physics.

units.la: 7. Mare meteoron esse negamus.
units.tr: 7. We deny that the sea is a meteor.

units.la: 8. Anima in intelligendo non utitur corporeo instrumento.
units.tr: 8. The soul in understanding does not use a bodily instrument.

units.la: 9. Intellectus & singularia, & universalia percipit.
units.tr: 9. The intellect perceives both singulars and universals.

units.la: 10. Male Aristoteles juvenes a philosophia morali arcet.
units.tr: 10. Aristotle wrongly keeps young men away from moral philosophy.

units.la: Τῷ Θεῷ δόξα.
units.tr: To God be the glory [Τῷ Θεῷ δόξα].

units.la: ORNATO ET DOCTO JUVENI Valentino Reussio, P.P.P.
units.tr: To the adorned and learned young man, Valentine Reuss, P.P.P.

units.la: VALENTINUS REUSSIUS
units.tr: VALENTINUS REUSSIUS

units.la: Ter μεταγραμματίζεται.
units.tr: Anagrammatised three times [μεταγραμματίζεται].

units.la: En utilis re, sanus usu.Usus in re sinus valet.Laetus in re, nisus usu.
units.tr: Behold, useful in the thing, sound in use. Use in the thing: the sinus prevails. Joyful in the thing, striving in use.

units.la: Quando Valentini vis nomina noscere Reussi,Nominis invertas vera elementa boni.Invenies sanum, certa utilitate probatum,Invenies usu, nomine reg; bonum.Usus inest rebus sinus, usus in arte probatur:Reusius hoc praestat, Reusius hoc q; valet.Nang; Valentini dum cognita nomina jactat,Omnibus in rebus recta valere probat.Nititur hoc usu, certa quoq; nititur arte,Subjectum Physices, quaerere quando juvat.Reusius hoc, vere mihi credite, nititur usu,Utilis hinc dici, nomine reg; solet.Est etiam verus quoniam verissima profertIn Thesibus doctis: Rumpere livor edax.Rumpere livor edax, verus verissima profert:Nil potis es contra: perside Mome vale.
units.tr: When you wish to know the names of Valentine Reuss, invert the true letters of the name of good. You will find him sound, proved by certain usefulness; you will find him good in use, and in name. Use dwells in the sinus of things; use is proved in the art. Reusius provides this, and Reusius is strong in this too. For while he boasts of the known names of Valentine, he proves that what is right prevails in all things. He rests on use, and rests also on a certain art, whenever it pleases you to inquire into the subject of physics. Reusius, believe me truly, rests on use, and is therefore wont to be called useful, and is named accordingly. He is also true, since he brings forth the most true things in his learned Theses: "Gnawing envy bursts." Gnawing envy bursts; the true man brings forth the most true things. You can do nothing against them: depart, Momus, and farewell.
